The previous world in this line of work delivered a complete paper on representation collapse in joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs): a theory in which collapse is decided early in training, near the collapsed solution, by a competition in every direction of representation space between a driving force that grows the direction and a decay effect that shrinks it, together with experiments that test it. That paper, its code and its results are in your repositories and workspaces. Take them as the starting point, not as the work to redo.

Extend that paper with the next piece of research on this problem. Begin from what it leaves open: its stated limitations, its predictions that were not tested or did not hold, the settings its theory does not reach (for example nonlinear or deep encoders, realistic data and architectures, training far from the collapsed solution), and what the theory implies for designing or choosing the heuristics that prevent collapse. Choose the directions that most advance the understanding of when and why JEPAs collapse, and carry them through to new theoretical or empirical results.

Deliver the extended paper, ready to submit to ICLR 2027 and written to the venue's submission requirements: the LaTeX source in the ICLR 2027 template, the compiled PDF, and the code and experimental results that the paper's claims rest on. Keep what still holds from the delivered paper, revise what the new results change, and make clear what the extension adds.

Do not use any paper, preprint, code release or other written work first published after 18 October 2026.

Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn representations by predicting the embedding of one part of an input from the embedding of another part, with no negative examples and no reconstruction loss. They are prone to representation collapse, in which the learned embeddings degenerate to a constant or to very low rank. In practice collapse is avoided with a collection of empirical heuristics (how the predictor is designed and scaled, how much of the input is masked, how the target encoder is updated), and no single account explains why they work. The insight to build on: collapse is decided early in training, near the collapsed solution, where two effects compete in every direction of representation space, a driving force that grows the direction and a decay effect that shrinks it. Whether a direction survives, and therefore how much rank the representation can develop, depends on which of the two is stronger there. The research problem is to turn this insight into a theory that explains and predicts when JEPAs collapse and what the common heuristics change, and to test that theory empirically.

Deliver a complete paper that could be submitted to NeurIPS 2026, written to the venue's submission requirements: the LaTeX source in the NeurIPS template, the compiled PDF, and the code and experimental results that the paper's claims rest on.

Do not use any paper, preprint, code release or other written work first published after 1 September 2026.

Three files are the study material: data.csv (40 points, columns x and y), figure.png and reference.pdf.

1. Fit a straight line y = a + b x to data.csv by ordinary least squares and report a and b, each with its 95% confidence interval.
2. figure.png and reference.pdf are part of the deliverable: keep both under outputs/ exactly as supplied, byte for byte, in the repository that holds the deliverable.
3. Write report/report.md, one page: the two coefficients with their intervals, the residual standard deviation, and one sentence on what each supplied file shows.

Nothing else is required.
